Book Review

The Late Great Planet Earth by Hal Lindsey. Bantam Books, New York, (30th printing) 1973. 180 pages, $1.25.

This fascinating book about Bible prophecies and the author's version of their modern fulfillment has gone through 30 impressions since its release in 1970 and boasts of having over 2 million copies in print. Lindsey has a pleasant, chatty style and has gathered a plethora of facts which supposedly support his major contention that Christianity is still relevant because the return of Christ is near. He makes use of the present anxiety over world affairs and points to matters as current as the daily paper as sure signs of the End.

The obvious problem with Lindsey's theory is that most of the ground he covers has been covered many times before in age after age. Eschatological speculation and millenialist expectation have occupied the minds of men since Jesus ended his mission. There have been untold hundreds of "prophets" who predicted doomsday for their own times. Bible scholars and Christian sects have used the very same verses quoted by Lindsey to predict the End for the years 1843, 1879 and 1914, among other dates. Some Christian sects currently warn that the End is sure to come in 1976. Lindsey himself leans toward 1988 (p. 43).

However, Lindsey is confident that he has found the one necessary histoircal ingredient missing in all previous predictions about the Last Day: the establishment of the state of "Israel" in the year 1948 (p. 33). The rebirth of "Israel" is the "fuse of Armageddon", the proof that our generation is living on borrowed time. But this conclusion produces in Lindsey's book the weird dogma best described as Christian Zionism. This states that Christ cannot come again and Christian hopes for the Kingdom of God cannot be fulfilled, until "Israel" is in complete control of Palestine, including Jerusalem, and the Temple of Solomon is rebuilt. "It is certain that the Temple will be rebuilt. Prophecy demands it," Lindsey argues on page 45. This puts him in the position of condoning the Israeli occupation of Palestine, the dispossession of the Arabs, Zionist terrorism against Palestinians and Zionist attempts to rebuild the Jewish Temple — which means the destruction of Qubbat al-Sakhrah. Of this he flippantly suggests, "Who knows, maybe there will be an earthquake." (p. 47) Man-made, perhaps???

Lindsey's Christian Zionism has uprooted the expected Christian compassion over the awful human misery of the refugee camps, the horrible napalming of Arab children by the Zionists and the terrible denial of Arab rights perpetrated by "Israel". But Christian Zionism has no basis in fact.

ISLAM 1394/1974, 1(2): 160-162
notes: Note the original spelling "histoircal" (apparent typo in the original printed text) preserved as printed. "Qubbat al-Sakhrah" is the Dome of the Rock, given without transliteration diacritics in the original for the sad. A faint gray show-through of the facing page's text is visible in the right margin.

Every one of the biblical verses which he quotes in support of it actually has reference to events a thousand years old, not to events of our day! For example, the prophet Ezekiel predicted the restoration of Israel and the reconstruction of the Temple about 598 B.C. His prophecy was fulfilled in 538 B.C., when the Jews returned from dispersal to Jerusalem and in 520 B.C., when the Temple was rebuilt. Thus, within 80 years of his prediction, Ezekiel's prophecy was completely fulfilled. To extend any part of his prophecy to our time, as Lindsey attempts to do, is idle speculation. What he calls "current history" is really ancient history!

The same is true regarding the New Testament prophecies of Jesus manipulated by Lindsey. Some of these are highly allegorical; others were fulfilled within a generation or two after Jesus' departure, such as the predictions of the destruction of the Jewish Temple and its desecration by the Romans. (Matthew, chapter 24) These things occurred between 70 and 134 C.E. After 134 C.E. the Romans made Jerusalem a colony, renamed Aelia, and forbade Jewish settlement there. The Temple site was rededicated to the Roman gods Jupiter and Zeus.

Rather than foretelling a Jewish return to Palestine, Jesus instead pronounced God's rejection of the Jews as a nation and God's abandonment of the Jewish Temple: "The kingdom of God will be taken away from you, and given to a nation that yields the proper fruit . . . O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that murders the prophets and stones the messengers sent to her . . . Look, look! there is your temple, forsaken by God." (Matthew 21:43 and 23:37, New English Bible) As the last prophet sent specifically to Israel, the verdict of Jesus carries infinitely more weight than Lindsey's conjectures and interpretations of the words of prior prophets.

There are also serious holes in Lindsey's argument that current history supports his interpretation of events marking the End. To cite just two of many examples, he predicts a Russian attack on "Israel" and the wholesale conversion of the Arabs to Communism. This looked plausible a few years back, before Nixonian detente and Kissingerian diplomacy, the Arab world is now making now. And, far from turning to Communism, the Arab world is now making overtures to the West.

Lindsey appears to have a real concern for the rebuilding of the Jewish Temple. He insists on it in several passages of his book. But this is impossible. For the Temple to be inaugurated anew, according to the Bible (Ezekiel 43:19-27), the priesthood must exist and the priesthood has not existed for 1900 years. This proves also that the Roman destruction of Jerusalem began in 70 C.E., after Jesus' warning to the Jews, was an act of Divine judgment on their nation. In previous tribulations, the priesthood had survived. But in 70 C.E. the Romans destroyed all the priestly records, in effect, destroying the priesthood. To this day, there is no priesthood in modern "Israel". There

can be no priesthood with the records which no longer exist. No priesthood, no Temple.

There are many prophecies in the Old Testament which were fulfilled with the coming of Jesus. His manner and place of birth, lineage, message and miracles were all recorded in advance so that believers would recognize him when he came. Lindsey is correct to charge the Jews with disobedience when they rejected Jesus despite these clear prophecies. But Christians, including Lindsey are guilty of doing exactly the same thing. The New Testament as well as the Old Testament contain many prophecies which were fulfilled with the coming of Muhammad. Similarly, prominent aspects of his lineage, personality, message and achievements were all recorded in advance. (See Islam, vol. I, no. 1, April 1974, pp. 1-13.) Christians have no more excuse for rejecting Muhammad than Jews have for rejecting Jesus (peace be upon them both), Jews and Christians are equally chargeable with persisting in the same error.

Rather than fantasizing over ancient history, Christians with a real interest in prophecy should heed the prophecy of Jesus concerning the P-R-KL-TOS (periklytos, Muhammad) who would come after him (John 14 and 16) who would reveal "the whole truth" and set the record straight. As a nation, the Jews have rejected both Jesus and Muhammad (peace be upon them). What, then, is the basis for any Divine favor upon a reborn Jewish nation? In surah Bani Isra'il (17:2-8) God shows that in the days of the prophet, the Jews had a last chance to return (since acceptance of Muhammad would mean acceptance of Jesus also, of whom Muhammad preached): "It may be that your Lord will yet show Mercy to you; but if you revert to your sins, We shall revert to our punishments, and We have made Hell a prison for those who reject faith." Again the nation chose disobedience.

The most insidious aspect of this book is its dogma that anyone who helps the Arab or Muslim cause against Zionism is courting the disfavor of God and sure disaster, regardless of the oppressive nature of Israeli occupation of Palestine. For Lindsey, the struggle against Zionism is tantamount to war against God!

But the fatal flaw in his whole attempt to promote Christian Zionism is that he himself finally shows its utter futility. After predicting that the Jews will be converted to belief in Christ just before the End (p. 156), he says, on the basis of his interpretation of prophecy, that only 1/3 of the Jews will be saved. The majority — 2/3 — will be lost. Therefore, according to Lindsey, even after Christ returns, even after God supposedly blesses Israeli aggression in Palestine, the majority of the Jews will go right on rejecting Jesus!

What a waste of 180 pages!

S. Shahid Mufassir

IT is held that when a Seeker gives his heart and mind to the search, and disperses the mists that arise from tumultuous passions, Truth becomes brighter and brighter and fills the Soul with its light.

It is asserted that while reason is puzzling itself about mystery of consciousness, time, and space, the man of Faith is going forward from discovery to discovery, in the growing illumination of his heart.

But it must be recognised that this knowledge is only available to those whose eyes are fixed, like an archer, on the arrow and the object at which he aims, and that without purity of purpose and unceasing effort deliverance cannot be obtained.

In all ages and in all times men have sought and found truth. They have shown the way and means of attainment. But men have listened to the message with incredulity and continued the mad pursuit of sense objects.

Passions of body and mind govern men and kindle fires of desire, of greed, attachment, egoism and anger. These enslave and obscure the mind which must be freed, and restored to its pristine purity to reflect truth. The seekers of truth, therefore, concentrate all their strength in drawing away the mind from sense objects and to set it free from the dominations of fear and hate. Some follow the path of knowledge, and others the path of devotion, hoping to lose all sense of duality in the supreme uprising of love.

(from Preface of "The Invocations of 'Abdullah Ansari")
